title: That our affections carry themselves beyond us
paragraphs: Those who accuse mankind of the folly of gaping after future things, and advise us to make use of the present and rest content with it on the ground that we have no grip on what is to come, even less than we have on what is past, have put their finger on the most universal of human errors — if it can be called an error, since nature herself has put it in us, for the continuation of her own work, planting in us, among other things, this deceiving imagination, more jealous of our acting than afraid of our knowing.

We are never with ourselves; we are always somewhere beyond. Fear, desire, hope keep pushing us toward the future, and meanwhile rob us of the sense and consideration of what is, to amuse us with the thought of what shall be — even when we shall be no more.
"Calamitosus est animus futuri anxius."
["The mind anxious about the future is miserable." — Seneca, Epist., 98.]

We find this great rule repeated often in Plato: "Do your own work, and know yourself." Each part contains all our duty between them, and each in its way involves the other; for whoever will do his own work properly will find that his first lesson is to know what he is and what is proper to him, and whoever rightly understands himself will never mistake another man's work for his own — he will love and improve himself above all else, refuse superfluous employments, and put aside all useless thoughts and propositions. As folly, on one side, even if it had everything it desired, would never be content, so wisdom, settling for what is present, is never dissatisfied with itself. Epicurus excuses his sages from all foresight and care of the future.

Among the laws relating to the dead, I think this a very sound one: that the actions of princes be examined after their death. They are equal with the laws, when not above them, and therefore what justice could not inflict on their persons it is only reasonable should fall on their reputations and on the estates of their successors — things we often value above life itself. This is a custom of singular advantage to the countries that use it, and one all good princes should welcome, for they have reason to be offended that the memories of the wicked should be treated with the same reverence as their own. We owe submission and obedience to all our kings, good or bad alike, for that has to do with their office; but esteem and affection are owed only to their virtue. Grant to political government that we endure unworthy rulers with patience, conceal their vices, and lend our recommendation to their indifferent actions while their authority still needs our support. But once the relation of prince and subject is over, there is no reason to deny our true opinions their voice, in the name of liberty and common justice; least of all to deny good subjects the glory of having served reverently and faithfully a prince whose imperfections they knew very well, since that would be to deprive posterity of a useful example. And those who, out of some private obligation, unjustly take up and defend the memory of a faulty prince serve a private interest at the cost of public justice. Livy says, very truly, that the language of men brought up in courts is always full of vain display and false witness: every one indifferently exalts his own master and stretches his praise to the utmost extent of virtue and sovereign greatness. Some may condemn the boldness of those two soldiers who answered Nero so roundly to his face. The one, asked why he hated him, said: "I loved you while you were worth it. Since you have become a parricide, an incendiary, a player, and a coachman, I hate you as you deserve." And the other, asked why he had tried to kill him, said: "Because I could think of no other remedy against your endless mischief." But the public, universal testimony given of Nero after his death (and which will go on being given of him, and of every other wicked prince like him, to all posterity) of his tyrannies and abominable conduct — who, in his sound judgment, can object to it?

I am offended that in a government as sacred as that of the Lacedaemonians there should have been mixed in so hypocritical a ceremony at the funeral of their kings — where all their allies, all their neighbours, and all kinds and ranks of men and women, including their slaves, cut and slashed their foreheads as a sign of grief, crying and lamenting that this king (even if he had been as wicked as the devil himself) was the best they had ever had. The effect is to attribute to his rank the praise that belongs only to merit, and that is properly owed to supreme worth even when it is found in the lowest and least placed subject.

Aristotle, who must have a finger in everything, raises a question about Solon's saying that no one can be called happy until he is dead: whether someone who has lived and died according to his heart's desire, but has left a bad name behind him and a miserable line of descendants, can really be called happy. As long as we have life and movement we can carry ourselves in fancy and preoccupation wherever we please; but once we are out of being, we have no further communication with what is — and so Solon would have done better to say that no one is ever happy, since he cannot really be so until he is no more.
"Quisquam Vix radicitus e vita se tollit, et eicit; Sed facit esse sui quiddam super inscius ipse, Nec removet satis a projecto corpore sese, et Vindicat."

["Scarcely any man can, even when dying, wholly detach himself from the idea of life; in his ignorance he imagines that something of himself survives, and cannot fully separate himself from his discarded body, or set himself free of it." — Lucretius, iii. 890.]

Bertrand du Guesclin, dying at the siege of the Castle of Rancon, near Le Puy in Auvergne, the besieged were ordered after surrender to lay the keys of the place upon the dead general's body. When Bartolommeo d'Alviano, the Venetian general, happened to die in the service of the Republic at Brescia, and his body had to be carried through the territory of Verona — enemy country — most of the army was inclined to ask the Veronese for safe-conduct. Theodoro Trivulzio opposed it, preferring to force a passage by arms and risk a battle, saying it was not fitting that one who had never feared his enemies in life should seem to fear them in death. Under Greek law, in fact, anyone who applied to an enemy for a body to bury it forfeited his victory and could no longer set up a trophy, while the one applied to was reckoned the winner. By this Nicias lost the advantage he had visibly gained over the Corinthians; and Agesilaus, by the same rule, secured an advantage over the Boeotians that he had only doubtfully earned in the field.

These things might seem strange if it had not been the general practice in every age, not only to extend our concern with ourselves beyond this life, but to imagine that heaven's favour does not merely often accompany us to the grave but, after life is over, takes an interest in our ashes. There are so many ancient examples of this — leaving aside what we see in our own time — that I need not labour the point. Edward I, King of England, in his long wars against Robert, King of Scotland, had experience of how decisive his own presence in person was to the success of his enterprises, having always been victorious in whatever he undertook in person; when he was dying he bound his son by solemn oath that as soon as he was dead his body should be boiled until the flesh came off the bones, and the flesh buried while the bones were preserved to be carried with the army whenever it had to march against the Scots — as if destiny had inevitably attached victory even to his remains. John Zizka, the same man who, in defence of Wycliffe's heresies, threw the Bohemian state into turmoil, left orders that he be flayed after his death and his skin made into a drum to be carried in war against his enemies, in the belief that it would contribute to the continuation of the successes he had always had against them. In the same way, certain of the Indians, in their battles with the Spaniards, carried with them the bones of one of their captains, on account of the victories they had once won under his command. And other peoples in that same New World carry with them in war the relics of brave men who had died in battle, to fire their courage and improve their luck. In the first kind of example, what was reserved for the tomb was only the reputation earned by past achievement; in the others, an active power is still attributed to the dead.

Captain Bayard's behaviour is of a better grain. Mortally wounded by a harquebus shot and pressed to retire from the fight, he answered that he would not begin at the last gasp to turn his back on the enemy. He fought on until, feeling himself too faint to sit on his horse, he ordered his steward to set him down at the foot of a tree — but so that he might die with his face toward the enemy, which he did.

I must add another example, no less striking than any of the rest for the present matter. The Emperor Maximilian, great-grandfather of the present King Philip, was a prince in whom great and uncommon qualities were everywhere mixed, including a singular personal beauty; but he had one habit very contrary to that of other princes, who for the despatch of their most important affairs turn the close-stool into a chair of state. He would not let any of his bedchamber, however familiar, see him in that posture, and would steal aside to make water as scrupulously as a virgin, shy of letting his physician or anyone else see those parts we are accustomed to conceal. I myself — for all the unembarrassed way I talk — am naturally so modest in this that, except under the pressure of necessity or pleasure, I scarcely ever let anyone see those parts or actions custom requires us to conceal: I suffer here more constraint than I think is becoming in a man, and especially in one of my profession. Maximilian fostered this modest humour to a degree of superstition: he gave express orders in his last will that they should put drawers on him as soon as he was dead — to which, I think, he might as well have added that the man who put them on should also be blindfolded. The charge Cyrus left with his children, that neither they nor anyone else should see or touch his body once the soul had left it, I put down to some superstitious devotion of his; for both Cyrus and his historian were noted throughout their great qualities for a singular respect and reverence for religion.

I was not at all pleased by a story told me, by a man of very great quality, about a relative of mine who had given a very good account of himself in peace and war: that coming to die in extreme old age, in excessive pain from the stone, he spent the last hours of his life in an extraordinary preoccupation with the honour and ceremony of his funeral. He pressed all the men of standing who came to see him to give their word to attend him to his grave; he importuned the prince himself, who came to visit him at his last gasp, with an earnest plea that he would order his household to be there; he laid out several arguments and examples to prove this was a respect due to a man of his condition; and he seemed to die content once he had obtained the promise and laid out the order and method of his funeral parade. I have seldom heard of so persistent a vanity.

Another, contrary curiosity (and there is no shortage of examples in my own family) seems somehow akin to this one: that a man should rack his brains in his last moments to plan obsequies of so peculiarly studied a frugality as to have one servant with a lantern. I see this humour praised, and the arrangement of Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, who forbade his heirs to spend on his funeral even the common ceremonies usual on such occasions. Is it really temperance and frugality to avoid expense and pleasure when the use and knowledge of them is imperceptible to us? An easy and cheap reformation. If guidance were needed here, I would say that in this, as in every other action of life, each person ought to regulate the matter according to his fortune. The philosopher Lycon prudently told his friends to dispose of his body wherever they thought best, and as for the funeral, to make it neither too superfluous nor too mean. For my part, I would leave the ordering of this ceremony entirely to custom, and shall, when the time comes, leave it to the discretion of whoever has to do me that last office. "Totus hic locus est contemnendus in nobis, non negligendus in nostris"; and a saint said this, very holily: "Curatio funeris, conditio sepulturae: pompa exequiarum, magis sunt vivorum solatia, quam subsidia mortuorum." Which made Socrates answer Crito, who asked him at his death how he wished to be buried: "However you like." If I were to occupy myself beyond the present with this affair at all, I should be most tempted, as the highest pleasure of this kind, to imitate those who in their lifetime entertain themselves with the ceremony and honours of their own obsequies in advance, and take pleasure in looking at their own dead face in marble. Happy are they who can gratify their senses by insensibility, and live by their death.

I am ready to feel an implacable hatred for every form of popular rule, though I think it the most natural and equitable of all, every time I remember the inhuman injustice of the people of Athens, who, without any hearing or vouchsafing the men a word in their defence, put to death their brave captains just returned in triumph from a naval victory they had won over the Lacedaemonians near the Arginusae Isles — the bloodiest and most stubborn engagement the Greeks ever fought at sea. The reason: that after the victory they had pressed their advantage according to the rule of war rather than stop to collect and bury their dead. The execution is the more odious for the behaviour of Diomedon, one of the condemned and a man of eminent virtue in both politics and arms. Once the sentence had been pronounced — no audience had been allowed until then — he stepped forward to speak, and instead of pleading his own cause or arguing the impiety of so cruel a sentence, only expressed concern for his judges' welfare. He asked the gods to turn this sentence to their good, and prayed that, for his and his companions' failure to fulfil the vows they had made (which he then named) in thanks for so glorious a victory, the gods' anger might not fall on them. And so without more words he went courageously to his death.

Fortune punished them in kind a few years later. Chabrias, captain-general of their naval forces, had the better of Pollis, the Spartan admiral, at the Isle of Naxos, but lost the whole fruit of his victory, a thing of great importance to their affairs, in order not to fall under this example: rather than lose a few bodies of dead friends that were floating in the sea, he gave a host of living enemies the chance to sail away in safety — and they made the Athenians pay dearly afterwards for this unseasonable superstition.
"Quaeris, quo jaceas, post obitum, loco? Quo non nata jacent."
["You ask where you shall lie after death? Where things lie that were never born."] — Seneca, Troades, Chorus ii. 30.
This other line restores the sense of rest to a body without a soul:
"Neque sepulcrum, quo recipiatur, habeat: portum corporis, ubi, remissa humana, vita, corpus requiescat a malis."
["Let him have no tomb to receive him, no haven for his body where, life being gone, the body may rest from its troubles." — Ennius, in Cicero, Tusc. i. 44.]

As nature shows us, several dead things keep a hidden relation to life. Wine changes its flavour and colour in the cellar according to the changes and seasons of the vine it came from; and the flesh of venison alters its condition in the brine-tub, and its taste, according to the laws of the living flesh of its kind — so it is said.
